analysis.one_liner: Directs the consumer financial regulator to set accuracy standards for credit score models and study alternative data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Lynch in June 2021 with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write standards for validating the accuracy and predictive value of credit scoring models, and to review scoring models every two years and bar factors that don't improve accuracy. It would also require the CFPB to study how including non-traditional data — rent, utility, and telecom payments — in credit scores affects credit-invisible consumers, minority communities, rural residents, women, immigrants, and lower-income households [S2] [S3]. Millions of Americans have thin or no credit files, so the fairness of the formulas that decide their loan rates matters directly to their wallets.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with thin credit files, lower-income households, rural residents, immigrants, and minorities who are scored by formulas they cannot inspect and whose accuracy no federal agency currently validates. Anyone who shops for a mortgage, car loan, or credit card relies on these scores; the bill would force the models to prove they actually predict repayment, and let the regulator strike factors that don't [S3]. A CFPB study of alternative data could open the door to counting rent and utility payments, which would help the roughly one in five adults who are 'credit invisible' or unscorable.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFPB, within one year and in consultation with banking regulators, to set standards validating the accuracy and predictive value of every credit scoring model in use, before release and at regular intervals thereafter [S3].

Requires a CFPB review of scoring models at least every two years, with authority to prohibit factors that do not contribute to the model's accuracy — a direct check on arbitrary or unexplainable scoring inputs [S3].

Orders a CFPB study of how alternative modeling techniques and non-traditional data (rent, utility, telecom payments) affect people with no or minimal credit history, minorities, women, immigrants, rural and urban consumers, and those earning under 120% of area median income, with a report to Congress within one year [S3].

The findings section cites CFPB research that consumers avoid comparison shopping for loans out of fear it will hurt their scores, the kind of confusion the bill's oversight provisions are meant to address [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit scoring model developers and the credit bureaus and lenders who buy and use their models would bear the cost of regular validation and the risk that the CFPB bars certain factors or models. If compliance costs are passed through, some costs could show up in credit pricing; the bill's critics could also argue that slower approval of new models delays products that could help credit-invisible consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit scoring firms and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: New validation requirements and the CFPB's power to prohibit factors or whole models could slow the release of new scoring products, including models that use alternative data to help people build credit — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

The bill itself flags that including non-traditional data raises unresolved questions about privacy, security, consumer control over their information, and potential discriminatory effects; the study it orders exists precisely because the benefits and harms are uncertain [S3].

With zero cosponsors [S4], the bill carried no visible coalition, which itself signals that its approach — full CFPB validation authority over all scoring models — was not broadly accepted even among House Democrats.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit of knowing their loan terms rest on validated, demonstrably accurate formulas is real and ongoing, since a few points on a credit score can mean thousands of dollars on a mortgage. The costs — compliance burden on scoring firms and some regulatory drag on innovation — are real but modest, and the bill addresses the alternative-data uncertainty by ordering a study rather than mandating its use. On balance the design is careful, though its single-author origin and lack of cosponsors suggest it needed more buy-in to function as legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on June 24, 2021, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA) introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1] [S5].
No cosponsors joined [S4], and no further action was ever taken — the action history ends with the committee referral [S5].
As a result, the CFPB never gained the validation standards or the biennial review-and-prohibition authority the bill proposed, and no study of alternative data's impact was mandated [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit scoring model developers and credit bureaus, which continue to sell and use scoring models with no federal validation of their accuracy or review of their factors.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch (D-MA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with sole authority to schedule markups on the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee with no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4], so no party-level vote ever revealed where each party stood.

industries.industry: Credit scoring model developers (e.g. FICO and competitors)
industries.note: The bill would require regular federal validation of their models and give the CFPB power to bar factors or models that don't add predictive value. Their unvalidated product determines the price and availability of credit for ordinary consumers, so their interest in avoiding oversight runs against the public's interest in accurate scores.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and lenders who buy scores
industries.note: They would face new compliance costs and possible model changes, but also benefit if validated scores reduce disputes and errors. Lenders currently rely on scores no regulator has independently validated, which is the gap the bill aimed to close.

industries.industry: Alternative data providers (rent, utility, telecom payment data)
industries.note: The bill doesn't mandate their use but orders a study of whether including them helps credit-invisible consumers, which could later expand their market only if the data prove accurate and fair to consumers.
